This module links to resources that provide a practical workflow for
making maps in R with [`ggplot2`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/) and
modern spatial packages. The main focus is on vector data represented as
`sf` objects, including polygon boundaries, lines, and point locations.
It also introduces raster data and the `terra` package.

The goal is not to provide a complete GIS course. Instead, these
resources provide a starting point for mapping sampling locations,
adding spatial layers to figures, displaying spatial patterns in
biological data, and connecting observations to environmental data.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

- distinguish vector data (points, lines, and polygons) from raster data
- read common spatial data formats into R using functions from the
  packages `sf` and `terra`
- convert longitude and latitude columns into an `sf` point object
- add points, lines, and polygons as layers in a `ggplot2` map
- map variables to point and polygon aesthetics such as color, fill, and
  size
- identify the coordinate reference system (CRS) of a spatial object and
  transform objects when necessary

## Start here: layering spatial data with *sf* and *ggplot2*

Here's a first broad introduction to mapping in R [Drawing beautiful
maps programmatically with R, `sf`, and `ggplot2`, Part 1:
Basics](https://r-spatial.org/r/2018/10/25/ggplot2-sf.html)

Then here's another example you can work through, that does additional
things you may want to do: [Drawing maps with `sf` and `ggplot2`, Part
2: Layers](https://r-spatial.org/r/2018/10/25/ggplot2-sf-2.html)

These are good starting resources for the basic workflow for things you
may want to do when making maps in R. They demonstrates how to:

- create point data from longitude and latitude values (i.e., map your
  sites)
- convert a regular data frame to an `sf` object with `st_as_sf()`
- add point locations to polygon maps
- obtain and plot U.S. state and county boundaries
- label map features
- map an attribute to polygon fill

The examples use the `rnaturalearth` package for a world map and the
`maps` package for U.S. states and counties.

### Important reminder GIS shapefiles

- A GIS "shapefile" is actually a group of related files, not just the
  `.shp` file. You need to keep all the files `.shp`, `.shx`, `.dbf`,
  and `.prj` together in the same folder.

## Raster data with *terra*

Raster data represent spatially continuous information as a grid of
cells. Examples include elevation, temperature, precipitation, land
cover, and remote-sensing imagery. Each raster has important spatial
properties, including its extent, resolution, number of layers, and CRS.

### [(Tutorial) Introduction to Working with Raster Data in R](https://www.neonscience.org/resources/learning-hub/tutorials/introduction-working-raster-data-r#toggle-0)

This current NEON tutorial introduces raster structure, GeoTIFF files,
and the modern `terra` package. Students download a small LiDAR-derived
elevation raster, inspect its metadata, and plot it in R.

The tutorial currently requires a NEON API token for downloading the
example data. Follow the setup instructions on the tutorial page, and do
not place an API token directly in an R script that will be shared.

For the next step, work through [Raster 01: Plot Raster Data in
R](https://www.neonscience.org/resources/learning-hub/tutorials/plot-raster-data-r),
which focuses on exploring raster values and improving raster plots.

An ecology-focused alternative is [R-GIS for Ecology: Chapter 4, Raster
Data (`terra`
basics)](https://aterui.github.io/rgis-for-ecology/raster-data-terra-basics.html).
It uses `terra` and demonstrates how raster and vector layers can be
plotted together with `ggplot2`.

### [(Another Tutorial) Introduction to rasters with `terra` from a lab at UCSB](https://emlab-ucsb.github.io/intro-terra/)

### [tidyterra Official Vignettes & Reference](https://dieghernan.github.io/tidyterra/)

- In older tutorials, plotting a raster in ggplot2 required converting
  the raster to a massive data frame via as.data.frame(r, xy = TRUE) and
  calling geom_raster(). Modern workflows use the tidyterra package to
  plot SpatRaster objects directly—automatically handling CRS alignment,
  downsampling for large grids, and color scales.

## Additional mapping resources

### [Maps: `ggplot2`, Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis](https://ggplot2-book.org/maps.html)

This chapter from the current online edition of the *ggplot2* book
provides a concise reference for the plotting concepts used in the
earlier tutorial. It covers:

- polygon maps and simple-feature maps;
- layered maps using multiple `geom_sf()` calls;
- labels with `geom_sf_text()` and `geom_sf_label()`;
- adding ordinary `ggplot2` layers such as `geom_point()` to a spatial
  map;
- map projections and coordinate reference systems; and
- working with raster maps.

## Obtaining map boundaries (country/state outlines) in R

Two useful packages for obtaining polygon boundaries are `rnaturalearth`
and `tigris`. They overlap in some uses, but they are designed for
different types of map data.

### *rnaturalearth*: broad global map data

`rnaturalearth` provides generalized map data from Natural Earth. It is
useful for world maps, countries, and broad administrative boundaries at
small to medium map scales. It is convenient for an introductory map
because the data can be returned directly as an `sf` object:

``` r
world <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries(
  scale = "medium",
  returnclass = "sf"
)

ggplot2::ggplot(world) +
  ggplot2::geom_sf()
```

Natural Earth data are generalized for cartographic use. They are
usually not the best choice for detailed U.S. county, tract, road, or
Census-data maps.

### *tigris*: detailed U.S. Census geographies

`tigris` downloads TIGER/Line or cartographic-boundary files from the
U.S. Census Bureau and returns them as `sf` objects. It is useful when
you need U.S.-specific boundaries, selectable data vintages, or detailed
geographies such as states, counties, census tracts, roads, water
features, and tribal areas.

``` r
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)

states <- tigris::states(cb = TRUE)
california_counties <- tigris::counties(
  state = "CA",
  cb = TRUE
)
```

Compared with `rnaturalearth`, `tigris` is usually better for
U.S.-specific analyses and spatial joins with Census or other U.S. data.
It can return more detailed files, so downloads may be larger and maps
may require more attention to the geographic vintage, resolution, and
treatment of Alaska and Hawaii.

See the [CRAN documentation for
`tigris`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=tigris) and [Analyzing U.S.
Census Data with R](https://walker-data.com/census-r/) for additional
examples.

## Spatial data concepts, file formats, and coordinate systems

- [Spatial data in R: Paula Moraga, *Spatial Statistics for Data
  Science*](https://www.paulamoraga.com/book-spatial/spatial-data-in-r.html)\
  Introduces vector and raster data, shapefiles, GeoTIFFs, `sf`,
  `terra`, and coordinate reference systems.

- [`sf` vignette: Reading, Writing, and Converting Simple
  Features](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/articles/sf2.html)\
  Reference documentation for reading and writing shapefiles, GeoJSON,
  GeoPackages, and other spatial formats.

- [`sf` vignette: Manipulating Simple
  Features](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/articles/sf4.html)\
  Shows how `sf` objects work with `dplyr`, including ordinary joins and
  spatially structured data manipulation.

- [Geocomputation with R: Geographic Data in
  R](https://r.geocompx.org/spatial-class)\
  A more detailed introduction to vector and raster data structures,
  spatial data models, and basic mapping.

- [Geocomputation with R: Spatial Data
  Operations](https://r.geocompx.org/spatial-operations)\
  Introduces spatial joins with `st_join()`, such as adding the county
  or habitat polygon containing each sampling location.

- [Geocomputation with R: Raster-Vector
  Interactions](https://r.geocompx.org/raster-vector)\
  Explains how to crop and mask rasters, extract raster values at points
  or polygons, and combine raster and vector data for analysis.

- [R-GIS for Ecology: Vector-Raster
  Interactions](https://aterui.github.io/rgis-for-ecology/vector-raster-interactions.html)\
  Ecology-focused examples of extracting precipitation values at fish
  survey sites and combining raster and vector data.

## Complete books and longer references

- [Geocomputation with R](https://r.geocompx.org/)\
  A comprehensive, free online book covering `sf`, `terra`, spatial data
  manipulation, spatial joins, raster-vector interactions, and links to
  GIS software.

- [Spatial Statistics for Data Science: Theory and Practice with
  R](https://www.paulamoraga.com/book-spatial/index.html)\
  A free online book by Paula Moraga. The early chapters provide useful
  background on spatial data, `sf`, `terra`, map-making, and packages
  for downloading open spatial data. Later chapters introduce spatial
  statistics, spatial models, and point-pattern analysis.

- [Spatial Data Science with R and `terra`](https://rspatial.org/)\
  Additional reference material for raster and vector spatial data
  analysis using the modern `terra` package.
